buildUp: Start with a fire in a box and surround it with water, so as much heat as possible goes straight into boiling it.
The firebox alone can't heat enough water, so run tubes from it through a long water-filled barrel, carrying the hot gases forward to a smokebox at the front.
Collect steam from the top of the boiler, dry and superheat it, and let the driver control its flow to two cylinders with a regulator.
Turn the pistons' push into rotation with connecting rods and cranks, and couple three pairs of big driving wheels together for grip.
Blast the used steam up the chimney to draw the fire, and use valve gear so the driver can choose how much steam each stroke takes, and run forwards or backwards.
Add a swivelling four-wheeled bogie at the front to guide it into curves at speed, and trailing wheels at the back so the firebox can be wide.
Finally, pull a tender behind with coal and water for a long run, and a cab where the crew can fire the boiler and drive.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Burn coal to boil water in a closed boiler, so the steam builds up pressure, then let that steam push pistons back and forth and turn the wheels through rods. Use the exhaust steam to fan the fire, so the harder the engine works the hotter it burns. Everything else, from the six coupled driving wheels to the swivelling bogie and the tender, exists to turn that pressure into steady, controllable pulling power at speed.

hardParts.title: A fire box full of pressure
hardParts.why: The firebox has flat walls holding back 15 bar of boiling water with a fire of over 1,000 °C inside. Flat plates bulge under pressure, so they're tied together by thousands of stays, and they must never run dry: if the water level drops below the firebox top, it overheats and can explode. Copper inner fireboxes conducted heat superbly but were expensive and wore out.

hardParts.title: Balancing the to-and-fro
hardParts.why: The heavy pistons and rods swing to and fro so fast that they can never be fully balanced, and any compromise either lets the engine sway or hammers the rails. Pistons and rods weighing hundreds of kilograms reverse direction about fourteen times a second at 100 mph. Weights in the wheels balance their rotating parts, but the back-and-forth parts can only be partly balanced; too little weight and the engine surges and sways, too much and the wheels hammer the rails once per turn.

hardParts.title: Getting the boiler to steam
hardParts.why: The blastpipe, chimney and tube sizes are a delicate balance: too narrow a nozzle wastes power pushing out exhaust, too wide and the fire won't draw. It matters because an engine is only as fast as its boiler can make steam, and that depends on how well the blast draws the fire through the tubes. Designers often tuned them by trial on the road, and the A3s improved markedly with double chimneys decades after they were built.

principles.explanation: Water swells enormously when it boils, so boiling it inside a sealed boiler builds up huge pressure, and that pressure is what pushes the pistons. A litre of water turns into about 1,600 litres of steam at normal air pressure. Trap it in a sealed boiler and it can't expand, so the pressure climbs instead, and the boiling point rises with it: at the A3's 15 bar, water doesn't boil until about 200 °C. Let that high-pressure steam into a cylinder and it pushes the piston with a force of around 30 tonnes. The boiler is really a store of hot, pressurised energy waiting to expand.
principles.title: Water expands enormously when it boils

principles.explanation: A piston can only push in a straight line, but a connecting rod joined to a pin set out from a wheel's centre turns that push into rotation, the same way your leg turns a bicycle pedal. At each end of the stroke the rod pushes straight through the axle and can't turn it, so the two sides' cranks are set a quarter turn apart. One side is always pushing hard, so the engine can start from any position.
principles.title: A crank turns pushing into turning

principles.explanation: The used steam is blasted up the chimney in a way that draws air through the fire, so the harder the engine works, the harder the fire burns and the more steam it makes. It leaves the cylinders through a narrow nozzle, and that fast jet drags air out of the smokebox, lowering its pressure, so air is pulled in through the fire and hot gases through the tubes. This self-regulating feedback is what made locomotives practical, ever since Stephenson's Rocket in 1829.
principles.title: The exhaust fans the fire

principles.explanation: How hard an engine can pull without slipping depends on the weight on its driving wheels, which is why this one couples three axles and loads them heavily. A steel wheel can only push on a steel rail with a force of about a quarter of the weight pressing it down before it slips. To pull a heavy train you need lots of weight on driving wheels, so coupling rods link three axles together and the engine puts about 65 tonnes on them. Making the wheels big, about 2 m across, means fewer piston strokes for each kilometre, so the engine can run fast without its moving parts flying apart.
principles.title: Grip comes from weight on the driving wheels

firstPrinciples.problem: Haul a 400-tonne express train hundreds of kilometres at over 100 km/h, using nothing but coal and water you can carry with you. The engine must make enormous power, grip the rails without slipping on two thin strips of steel, take curves without derailing, and fit under bridges and through tunnels built for much smaller trains, all while a crew of two keeps it fed and under control.

questions.answer: Each turn of a big wheel covers more ground, so at high speed the pistons and rods move back and forth fewer times a second. Freight engines want pulling power rather than speed, and smaller wheels give each piston stroke more leverage on the rails.
questions.question: Why do express locomotives have much bigger driving wheels than freight locomotives?

questions.answer: At the very ends of its stroke a piston pushes straight through the axle and can't turn it. With the other side a quarter turn out of step, one piston is always mid-stroke, so the engine can start wherever it stopped.
questions.question: Why are the cranks on the left and right sides set a quarter of a turn apart?

questions.answer: Each chuff is a blast of used steam from a cylinder going up the chimney. Working hard means more steam per stroke, so the blasts are stronger, and those blasts also draw the fire harder to make more steam.
questions.question: Why does a steam engine "chuff" louder when it's working hard?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The steam locomotive's genius is the feedback loop in the smokebox: the exhaust that leaves the cylinders is the same blast that draws the fire, so the engine automatically burns harder exactly when it works harder. Add a crew who read the fire, the water and the road ahead, and a 150-tonne engine and tender with only a few percent efficiency could still run a heavy train non-stop from London to Edinburgh, or touch 126 mph.

name: Steam Locomotive
overview:
A steam locomotive is a travelling power station. The fireman shovels coal into a firebox at the back of the boiler, the hot gases rush forward through dozens of tubes running the length of the barrel, and the water around those tubes boils. The steam collects at the top, is dried and superheated, and is let into the cylinders by the driver's regulator. There it pushes pistons back and forth, and rods turn that motion into the turning of the driving wheels.

The name "4-6-2" counts the wheels from the front: four small wheels on a swivelling bogie to guide the engine into curves, six big driving wheels coupled together by rods, and two trailing wheels under the cab to carry the wide firebox. Engines with this layout were nicknamed "Pacifics" and became the classic express passenger locomotive in Britain, America and beyond in the first half of the twentieth century. Big driving wheels let the pistons stay at a sensible speed while the train runs fast.

Behind the engine is the tender, which carries the coal and the water, about 9 tonnes of coal and 5,000 gallons (about 23,000 litres) of water on the LNER's big express tenders. A locomotive uses water much faster than coal, and some tenders could scoop it up from troughs between the rails without stopping. The LNER A3 Flying Scotsman was the first steam locomotive officially recorded at 100 mph, in 1934, and its streamlined cousin, the A4 Mallard, still holds the world speed record for steam at 126 mph (203 km/h), set in 1938.

parts.description: Long tapered steel drum full of water, heated by the hot gases flowing forward through its tubes.

details.didYouKnow: If a boiler's water ever ran too low, the top of the firebox could overheat and give way, letting the whole boiler flash into steam at once; that's why the crew watch the water-level glass constantly.
details.howItWorks: The barrel is a long steel drum filled with water almost to the top, with the firebox at the back and the smokebox at the front. Hot gases from the fire pass forward through tubes running its whole length, and the water around them boils. The steam gathers in the space above the water at a pressure of about 15 bar, and the taper puts the most water and steam over the hottest end, by the firebox.
keyNumbers: About 1.9 m across at its widest
Roughly 6 m long between the firebox and smokebox
Working pressure about 15 bar (220 psi on an A3)
Water inside boils at about 200 °C at that pressure
details.madeOf: Rolled steel plates about 2 cm thick, riveted or welded into rings, wrapped in insulation and covered with thin painted steel sheets called cladding.

parts.name: Boiler barrel

parts.description: Bundle of tubes carrying the fire's hot gases through the water, with superheater elements in the larger flues.

details.didYouKnow: Tubes clog with soot and ash, so at the shed a cleaner blows them through with a steam lance, and on the road the fireman sometimes threw sand into the fire so the blast scoured them clean.
details.howItWorks: The tubes are the boiler's radiator in reverse: the fire's hot gases flow through them while water surrounds them, so heat passes through thin metal into a huge area of water. The larger flues each carry a superheater element, a looped pipe that takes the steam back through the hot gases to dry it and heat it well above its boiling point. Superheated steam doesn't condense in the cylinders, which saves a lot of water and coal.
keyNumbers: Over 100 small tubes plus about 40 larger flues on an A3
Steam superheated to roughly 350 to 400 °C
Superheating can save around a fifth of the coal and water
details.madeOf: Seamless steel tubes expanded into holes in the firebox and smokebox tube plates, with steel superheater elements inside the larger flues.

parts.name: Fire tubes & superheater

parts.description: Drum at the front where the spent steam blasts up the chimney, drawing the fire through the tubes.

details.didYouKnow: The famous "chuff" of a steam engine is the exhaust blast in the smokebox; you can tell how hard an engine is working, and whether its valves are set evenly, just by listening to it.
details.howItWorks: The smokebox is the front chamber where the tubes end. The used steam from the cylinders shoots straight up through a nozzle called the blastpipe and out of the chimney, and each blast drags the smoke and gases with it, leaving a partial vacuum behind. That vacuum sucks air through the fire and gases through the tubes, so the harder the engine works, the fiercer the fire burns.
keyNumbers: About 1.9 m across
Four exhaust beats for every turn of the driving wheels on a two-cylinder engine
Pulls a vacuum of only about 1 to 2 percent of atmospheric pressure
details.madeOf: Heavy steel plate, painted black with heat-resistant paint because it gets very hot, holding the blastpipe, superheater header and steam pipes.

parts.name: Smokebox

parts.description: Round, airtight front door opened at the shed to shovel out the ash and char drawn through the tubes.

details.didYouKnow: A smokebox door that glows or shows a scorched patch of paint is a warning sign: air leaking in lets hot char burn right there at the front.
details.howItWorks: The round door closes the front of the smokebox and must seal well, because any air leaking in spoils the vacuum that draws the fire. It's held shut by a central handle and dart that locks onto a crossbar inside, and opens on hinges like a big round porthole. At the end of a run, the crew open it to shovel out the char and ash sucked through the tubes.
keyNumbers: About 1.7 m across
Locked by one central dart and a pair of handles
Must stay airtight under a small vacuum
details.madeOf: Pressed steel plate, dished for stiffness, with a ring of heat-resistant seal, steel hinges and handles, often with a numberplate fixed to it.

parts.name: Smokebox door

parts.description: Short chimney, kept low to fit under bridges, that the exhaust steam and smoke shoot out of.

details.didYouKnow: In the late 1950s the A3s were fitted with Kylchap double chimneys, which split the blast into two streams and made them faster and more economical, but the softer exhaust then drifted down over the cab.
details.howItWorks: The chimney takes the mixed exhaust steam and smoke from the blastpipe and throws it upwards, away from the engine. Its tapering shape works with the blastpipe nozzle like a pump, so the jet of steam drags as much gas as possible out of the smokebox. On British railways it had to be short, because bridges and tunnels left very little room above the boiler.
keyNumbers: Top roughly 4 m above the rails, the limit of the British loading gauge
About 0.4 m tall above the smokebox
Later A3s carried a double chimney with two blastpipes
details.madeOf: Cast iron or fabricated steel, with a liner or petticoat inside that guides the blast and sets how well the engine steams.

parts.name: Chimney

parts.description: Raised cover on top of the boiler where the driest steam is collected, high above the water.

details.didYouKnow: Gresley's A3s used a long, banjo-shaped steam collector instead of a tall round dome, perforated along its top to gather the driest steam from a wide area.
details.howItWorks: The dome is a raised housing on top of the barrel that collects steam from as high as possible above the boiling water. Taking steam from up there means less water is carried over into the pipes as spray, which could damage the cylinders. Inside it sits the regulator valve, opened by the driver's handle in the cab through a long rod.
keyNumbers: About 0.8 m across
Raises the steam intake well above the water level
Holds the regulator valve on many engines
details.madeOf: A pressed steel dome base riveted to the boiler, with a painted steel or brass cover on top; the regulator valve inside is cast iron or bronze.

parts.name: Steam dome

parts.description: Spring-loaded valves that blow off steam with a roar if the pressure rises above the safe limit.

details.didYouKnow: Crews hated "blowing off": every roar from the safety valves was water and coal going straight up into the sky, so a good fireman kept pressure just below the blowing-off point.
details.howItWorks: Each valve is held shut by a stiff spring. If the steam pressure rises past the set limit, it overcomes the spring and the valve pops open, blowing steam off with a deafening roar until the pressure falls back. There are two, so the boiler is still protected if one sticks.
keyNumbers: Two valves for safety
Set to lift at the boiler's working pressure, about 15 bar
Can release steam faster than the fire can make it
details.madeOf: Gunmetal or bronze bodies with steel springs, seated on top of the firebox where the steam space is.

parts.name: Safety valves

parts.description: Box at the back of the boiler, surrounded by water, where the coal burns on a grate.

details.didYouKnow: Firebox stays are drilled with a small tell-tale hole down their middle; if one cracks, steam whistles out of the hole and warns the crew before anything gives way.
details.howItWorks: The firebox is a box inside a box: the inner one holds the fire on a grate of iron bars, and the space between the inner and outer walls is filled with water. That water is heated directly by the fire, so the firebox makes a large share of the steam even though it's much shorter than the barrel. A wide firebox like this one sits above the trailing wheels, giving room for a big grate.
keyNumbers: Grate area about 3.8 m² on an A3
Fire burning at well over 1,000 °C
Inner and outer walls tied by roughly 2,000 stays
details.madeOf: An inner box of copper, which conducts heat superbly, held to the steel outer box by thousands of threaded stays that stop the flat walls bulging under pressure.

parts.name: Firebox

parts.description: Tall plate beside the smokebox that steers air upwards, lifting the smoke clear of the driver's view.

details.didYouKnow: These angled deflectors on the A3s were nicknamed "German" or "trough" deflectors because their style was copied from locomotives in Germany.
details.howItWorks: At speed the air flowing over a smooth boiler can let the soft exhaust roll down along the sides and hide the line ahead. The left deflector catches air rushing past the front and turns it upwards, creating a draught that lifts the smoke clear of the boiler. That keeps the driver's view of signals clear.
keyNumbers: About 1.9 m long and 1.3 m tall
Stands a short distance out from the smokebox
Fitted to A3s from about 1960
details.madeOf: Thin steel plate on brackets bolted to the running plate and smokebox, painted to match the engine.

parts.name: Smoke deflector (left)

parts.description: Tall plate beside the smokebox that steers air upwards, lifting the smoke clear of the driver's view.

details.didYouKnow: Some engines were given small ones, some big ones and some none at all; designers often only discovered whether smoke would drift by trying the engine out on the line.
details.howItWorks: The right deflector mirrors the left, so the air is guided upwards on both sides of the smokebox and the smoke rises straight above the boiler. Without the pair, a crosswind could blow smoke down one side or the other. The driver on these engines sits on the right, so this side matters most for seeing ahead.
keyNumbers: One of a matched pair
Shaped to work at express speeds
Weighs only a few tens of kilograms
details.madeOf: Thin steel plate, stiffened at the edges, painted in the engine's livery.

parts.name: Smoke deflector (right)

parts.description: Curved steel roof sheltering the driver and fireman, with a sliding vent to let the heat out.

details.didYouKnow: On a hot day the footplate in front of the open firehole could be fierce, while on a cold night the crew's backs froze in the draught, so cab comfort was a constant complaint.
details.howItWorks: The roof shelters the driver and fireman from rain and gives some shade from the heat pouring off the firebox. A sliding or hinged vent in the middle lets the hot air escape. It overhangs at the back towards the tender to give a bit more cover over the open footplate.
keyNumbers: About 2.3 m long
Top kept under about 4 m to clear bridges
Footplate temperatures could pass 40 °C in summer
details.madeOf: Curved steel sheet on steel ribs, painted black or in livery, with a sliding ventilator.

parts.name: Cab roof

parts.description: Side sheet of the cab with a window; the crew lean out of the opening to see ahead past the long boiler.

details.didYouKnow: Crews often looked out through the narrow side gap at speed, protected by the little hinged glass screen, because looking forward through the small front windows past the boiler showed very little.
details.howItWorks: The left side sheet encloses the fireman's side of the cab, with a window to look out of and an opening to lean through. On British engines like this one the fireman works on the left, and he watches for signals on curves where the driver's view is blocked by the long boiler. A fold-down seat sits on this side for the brief rests between firing.
keyNumbers: About 2 m long
Window opening at shoulder height
Fireman's side on Gresley's Pacifics
details.madeOf: Steel plate with a glass sliding window and a hinged glass draught screen.

parts.name: Cab side (left)

parts.description: Side sheet of the cab with a window; the crew lean out of the opening to see ahead past the long boiler.

details.didYouKnow: British signals mostly stand to the left of the line, so many railways moved their drivers to the left; Gresley's Pacifics kept the driver on the right, so the fireman called out signals on left-hand curves.
details.howItWorks: The right side sheet encloses the driver's side, where the regulator, reverser and brake handle are within reach. Gresley's engines were driven from the right, and the driver leans out of this side to spot signals ahead. Its shape matches the left side so the cab looks symmetrical.
keyNumbers: About 2 m long
Window opening at shoulder height
Driver's side on LNER engines
details.madeOf: Steel plate with a sliding window, painted to match the rest of the engine.

parts.name: Cab side (right)

parts.description: Front sheet of the cab wrapped round the firebox, with round lookout windows either side.

details.didYouKnow: Engine crews called the front cab plate the "spectacle plate", because its two round windows look like a pair of glasses.
details.howItWorks: The front sheet closes off the cab around the back of the firebox, which pokes through into the cab where the controls and the firehole are. Small round or angled windows on either side of the boiler let the crew see forward along the running plate. It also carries some gauges and pipework for the controls.
keyNumbers: About 2.75 m wide, the full width of the engine
Two lookout windows
Firebox back sits about 1 m inside the cab
details.madeOf: Steel plate cut to fit the firebox shape, with glass windows in frames that can be opened for cleaning.

parts.name: Cab front

parts.description: Door in the back of the firebox that the fireman opens to shovel coal onto the fire.

details.didYouKnow: On the 1928 non-stop runs from London to Edinburgh, two firemen, who swapped over halfway, shovelled roughly 8 tonnes of coal through this door between them in just over eight hours.
details.howItWorks: The firehole is the opening at the back of the firebox where the fireman shovels in coal, aiming each shovelful at a different part of the grate to keep the fire even. Between shovels the door is kept nearly shut so that cold air doesn't rush in and chill the tubes. A deflector plate inside steers incoming air over the fire so the smoke burns properly.
keyNumbers: About 0.4 m wide
Several tonnes of coal shovelled through it on a long run
Opened and closed for every shovelful
details.madeOf: Cast iron or steel doors on a frame riveted into the firebox backplate, with a lever or foot pedal to swing them open.

parts.name: Firehole door

parts.description: The locomotive's throttle: pulling it opens a valve that lets steam from the dome through to the cylinders.

details.didYouKnow: Good drivers often ran with the regulator wide open and controlled the engine mostly with the reverser, using the steam expansively and saving coal.
details.howItWorks: The regulator is the locomotive's throttle. Pulling the handle across opens a valve in the dome, letting steam into the main steam pipe, through the superheater and on to the cylinders. The driver controls the engine with this and the reverser, which sets how much of each piston stroke takes in steam.
keyNumbers: One handle controls the main steam supply
Opened gradually to avoid the wheels slipping
Used together with the reverser's cut-off setting
details.madeOf: A polished steel or brass handle on a shaft through the firebox backplate, linked by a long rod inside the boiler to the regulator valve.

parts.name: Regulator handle

parts.description: Screw on a column beside the driver that sets the valve gear, through a long reach rod, for forward, reverse and how early steam is cut off.

details.didYouKnow: Some engines used a simple lever instead of a screw, which was quicker to throw over but could kick back violently if the driver let go; the screw was gentler and allowed fine setting at speed.
details.howItWorks: The driver winds a handwheel on this column, and a screw moves a long reach rod running forward along the engine to the reversing shaft. That shaft lifts or lowers the radius rods in the expansion links on both sides, setting whether the engine runs forwards or backwards and how early in each stroke the valves shut off steam. Starting a heavy train, the driver sets a late cut-off for maximum push; once moving, he winds it back so the steam expands and does more work.
keyNumbers: Cut-off typically set between roughly 15% and 75%
Several turns of the wheel from full forward to full reverse
Reach rod runs most of the engine's length
details.madeOf: A cast-iron column with a steel screw and nut, a brass indicator scale, and a steel reach rod several metres long.

parts.name: Reverser

parts.description: Outside cylinder where steam pushes the piston first one way, then the other.

details.didYouKnow: The A3 and A4 actually had three cylinders, a third one hidden between the frames; many other Pacifics, like the British Railways Britannias, made do with these two outside ones.
details.howItWorks: Steam is let into the cylinder first at one end and then the other, so it pushes the piston forwards and then back with each turn of the wheels. A valve in the steam chest above times when steam enters and when it's let out to the blastpipe. Being outside the frames, it's easy to reach for maintenance.
keyNumbers: About 50 cm bore
Piston stroke roughly 66 to 71 cm
Full boiler pressure, about 15 bar, on the piston
details.madeOf: A thick casting of iron or steel, bored smooth inside, with drain cocks to let out water and a cladding sheet to keep the heat in.

parts.name: Cylinder (left)

parts.description: Piston sliding inside the cylinder, with a rod that carries its push out through a steam-tight gland to the crosshead.

details.didYouKnow: At 100 mph the piston reverses direction around fourteen times a second, slamming to a stop and starting again each time, which is why balancing the motion was such a challenge.
details.howItWorks: The piston is a thick disc with springy rings around its edge that seal against the cylinder wall, so steam can only push it and not leak past. Its rod passes out through a packed gland at the back of the cylinder to the crosshead, which slides along guide bars. The crosshead keeps the rod straight while the connecting rod swings up and down.
keyNumbers: Piston about 50 cm across
Travels back and forth about seven times a second at 100 mph
Rod roughly 1.5 m long to the crosshead
details.madeOf: A cast iron or steel piston head with iron rings, on a polished high-strength steel rod.

parts.name: Piston & rod (left)

parts.description: Heavy rod from the crosshead to a crank pin on the middle driving wheel, turning to-and-fro into round-and-round.

details.didYouKnow: The fluted or I-beam shape of the rods isn't for looks: it removes metal where it does little work, so the rod is lighter and puts less pounding on the track.
details.howItWorks: The connecting rod joins the crosshead to a crank pin on the middle driving wheel. As the crosshead slides back and forth, the rod's far end follows the crank pin round its circle, turning a straight push into rotation. It's the single rod that delivers all the power from this cylinder to the wheels.
keyNumbers: About 3.3 m long
Carries pushes and pulls of roughly 30 tonnes
Big end swings in a circle about 66 cm across
details.madeOf: Forged high-tensile steel, machined to an I-shaped section to be light but very stiff, with bronze bearings at each end.

parts.name: Connecting rod (left)

parts.description: Rod linking the crank pins of all three driving wheels so they turn together and share the grip.

details.didYouKnow: Driving wheels must all be exactly the same size, or the coupling rod would fight them; that's why tyres are turned on a wheel lathe in sets.
details.howItWorks: The coupling rod links the crank pins of all three driving wheels on the left, so whatever the connecting rod does to the middle wheel, the front and back wheels do too. That shares the drive among all six wheels, giving the grip of three axles rather than one. It's jointed so the wheels can still move up and down on their springs.
keyNumbers: About 4.4 m long
Links three driving wheels
Lets the engine put roughly 65 tonnes of weight onto the rails for grip
details.madeOf: Forged high-tensile steel, fluted for lightness, with bronze bushes on each crank pin.

parts.name: Coupling rod (left)

parts.description: Walschaerts valve gear: rods and a slotted link that time the valves letting steam in and out of the cylinder.

details.didYouKnow: Reducing the cut-off is called "notching up", from old reversing levers that locked into notches; an express might run at only 15% cut-off once up to speed.
details.howItWorks: Walschaerts valve gear takes motion from a small return crank on the middle wheel and from the crosshead, and combines them to slide the valve that feeds steam into the cylinder. A slotted, curved expansion link lets the driver choose how early the valve shuts off steam in each stroke, or reverse the engine completely. Shutting off early lets the steam expand and do extra work, saving coal.
keyNumbers: Cut-off adjustable from about 75% down to about 15% of the stroke
Same gear sets forward and reverse
Invented by Egide Walschaerts in 1844
details.madeOf: Forged and machined steel rods and links with hardened pins and bronze bushes.

parts.name: Valve gear (left)

parts.description: Sliding block that joins the piston rod to the connecting rod, running between guide bars that take the rod's sideways push.

details.didYouKnow: Crews checked slide bars and crossheads by hand at every stop, feeling for heat: a hot crosshead meant its oil supply had failed.
details.howItWorks: The piston rod can only push in a straight line, but the connecting rod swings up and down as the wheel turns, so its end pushes sideways too. The crosshead takes that sideways push, sliding between guide bars bolted to the back of the cylinder, and passes the straight push on to the connecting rod through a pin. It also drives the bottom of the valve gear's combination lever through a short drop arm.
keyNumbers: Travels the full piston stroke, roughly 66 cm on an engine like this
Reverses direction several times a second at speed
Slide bars take pushes of several tonnes
details.madeOf: Cast or forged steel with bronze or white-metal slippers where it rubs on the hardened steel slide bars, fed with oil.

parts.name: Crosshead & slide bars (left)

parts.description: Outside cylinder where steam pushes the piston first one way, then the other.

details.didYouKnow: Clouds of steam from the drain cocks when an engine starts aren't a leak: the driver opens them to blow out water that condensed in the cold cylinders, which would otherwise crack a cylinder cover.
details.howItWorks: The right cylinder works just like the left, but its crank is set a quarter of a turn apart from the left one. That way, when one piston is at the end of its stroke and can't push, the other is mid-stroke and pushing hardest. It means the engine can always start, whatever position the wheels stop in.
keyNumbers: About 50 cm bore
Crank set 90° from the left side
Each piston pushes with a force of roughly 30 tonnes
details.madeOf: Cast iron or steel, bored and fitted with steam-tight covers at each end and drain cocks underneath.

parts.name: Cylinder (right)

parts.description: Piston sliding inside the cylinder, with a rod that carries its push out through a steam-tight gland to the crosshead.

details.didYouKnow: Piston rings were invented for steam engines and are still used in almost every car engine today.
details.howItWorks: The right piston matches the left and is driven the same way, but always a quarter of a revolution out of step with it. Together they give four pushes for each turn of the wheels, which is what makes the four exhaust beats. Its rings wear slowly and are replaced at overhauls.
keyNumbers: Two pushes per wheel turn, one each way
Rings seal against about 15 bar of steam
Quartered 90° from the left piston
details.madeOf: Cast iron or steel head with cast iron piston rings, on a polished steel rod.

parts.name: Piston & rod (right)

parts.description: Heavy rod from the crosshead to a crank pin on the middle driving wheel, turning to-and-fro into round-and-round.

details.didYouKnow: A hot big-end bearing could melt its white metal at speed; some engines had a small capsule that released a smell of aniseed or garlic to warn the crew.
details.howItWorks: The right connecting rod drives the right-hand crank pin of the middle axle, a quarter turn out of step with the left. Because the two cranks on the same axle are set at 90°, the axle is pushed round smoothly instead of in jerks. Its bearings are oiled from small reservoirs on the rod.
keyNumbers: About 3.3 m long
Drives the middle of the three coupled axles
Big-end bearings checked by touch for heat at stops
details.madeOf: Forged high-tensile steel with bronze or white-metal bearings, oiled by hand before each trip.

parts.name: Connecting rod (right)

parts.description: Rod linking the crank pins of all three driving wheels so they turn together and share the grip.

details.didYouKnow: The nickname "Pacific" comes from some of the first 4-6-2s, built in the USA in 1901 for New Zealand, across the Pacific Ocean.
details.howItWorks: The right coupling rod does the same job on the other side, keeping all three right-hand driving wheels turning together. Its crank pins are a quarter turn ahead of or behind the left side's. With both rods, the six driving wheels act as a single, very grippy set.
keyNumbers: About 4.4 m long
Crank pins quartered 90° from the left side
Turns about seven times a second at 100 mph
details.madeOf: Forged high-tensile steel with bronze bushes, fluted to save weight.

parts.name: Coupling rod (right)

parts.description: Walschaerts valve gear: rods and a slotted link that time the valves letting steam in and out of the cylinder.

details.didYouKnow: On the A3s, Gresley worked the hidden middle cylinder's valve from the two outside valve gears using clever levers, saving a third set of gear.
details.howItWorks: The right-hand valve gear mirrors the left and is linked to it through a shaft across the engine, so the driver's reverser sets both sides together. Each valve has to be timed exactly to its piston, or the exhaust beats will sound uneven. Setting the valves correctly is a skilled fitter's job.
keyNumbers: Driven by a return crank on the middle wheel
Moves the valve a few tens of millimetres each way
Adjusted from the cab through the reversing screw
details.madeOf: Forged steel rods and expansion link, with hardened pins and bronze bushes, lubricated by oil.

parts.name: Valve gear (right)

parts.description: Sliding block that joins the piston rod to the connecting rod, running between guide bars that take the rod's sideways push.

details.didYouKnow: Crews checked slide bars and crossheads by hand at every stop, feeling for heat: a hot crosshead meant its oil supply had failed.
details.howItWorks: The piston rod can only push in a straight line, but the connecting rod swings up and down as the wheel turns, so its end pushes sideways too. The crosshead takes that sideways push, sliding between guide bars bolted to the back of the cylinder, and passes the straight push on to the connecting rod through a pin. It also drives the bottom of the valve gear's combination lever through a short drop arm.
keyNumbers: Travels the full piston stroke, roughly 66 cm on an engine like this
Reverses direction several times a second at speed
Slide bars take pushes of several tonnes
details.madeOf: Cast or forged steel with bronze or white-metal slippers where it rubs on the hardened steel slide bars, fed with oil.

parts.name: Crosshead & slide bars (right)

parts.description: Small guiding wheel on the front bogie, which swivels to lead the engine smoothly into curves.

details.didYouKnow: The leading bogie was an American idea from the 1830s, and it's why express engines could run so fast on curving track.
details.howItWorks: This small wheel is at the front left of the leading bogie, a four-wheeled truck that can swivel and slide sideways. As the engine meets a curve, the bogie turns first and guides the heavy engine smoothly into it. Without it, the big driving wheels would grind against the rails and could climb off them at speed.
keyNumbers: About 0.97 m diameter
Shares the front bogie's load of roughly 20 tonnes
Bogie can slide a few centimetres sideways
details.madeOf: A cast steel wheel centre with a separate hard steel tyre shrunk on, so worn tyres can be replaced.

parts.name: Bogie wheel (front, left)

parts.description: Small guiding wheel on the front bogie, which swivels to lead the engine smoothly into curves.

details.didYouKnow: Smaller wheels turn faster at the same speed, so bogie wheels spin roughly twice as fast as the driving wheels.
details.howItWorks: The rear left bogie wheel sits behind the front one on the same frame. Its axle and the front one pivot together around a central pin under the cylinders. Springs on the bogie keep it centred on straight track and let it ease sideways on curves.
keyNumbers: About 0.97 m diameter
Turns about 15 times a second at 100 mph
One of four bogie wheels
details.madeOf: Cast steel wheel centre with a shrunk-on steel tyre.

parts.name: Bogie wheel (rear, left)

parts.description: One of six 2-metre driving wheels; the pistons turn them through the rods and they push the train along.

details.didYouKnow: Big driving wheels mean fewer turns, and fewer piston strokes, for each kilometre, which is why express engines had huge wheels while freight engines had small ones for pulling power.
details.howItWorks: This is the front driving wheel on the left. It's turned by the coupling rod from the middle wheel and pushes against the rail to move the train. A weight cast into the wheel balances the rods so the engine doesn't shake itself apart at speed.
keyNumbers: About 2.03 m (6 ft 8 in) diameter
About 7 turns a second at 100 mph
Axle load around 22 tonnes
details.madeOf: A cast steel spoked centre with a steel tyre shrunk on, and a crescent-shaped balance weight between the spokes.

parts.name: Driving wheel (leading, left)

parts.description: One of six 2-metre driving wheels; the pistons turn them through the rods and they push the train along.

details.didYouKnow: Balance weights can't cancel the to-and-fro of the rods perfectly, so at speed the wheels pound the rail slightly once per turn, an effect called hammer blow.
details.howItWorks: The middle left wheel is the one the connecting rod drives directly, through a crank pin set out from its centre. All the power from this side's cylinder goes into this wheel first, and the coupling rod passes it on to the other two. Its balance weight is the biggest, because it has to counter the heavy rod as well.
keyNumbers: About 2.03 m diameter
Crank pin roughly 33 cm from the centre
Carries the connecting rod and coupling rod
details.madeOf: Cast steel spoked centre, steel tyre and a large balance weight, with a hardened steel crank pin pressed in.

parts.name: Driving wheel (middle, left)

parts.description: One of six 2-metre driving wheels; the pistons turn them through the rods and they push the train along.

details.didYouKnow: Wheel tyres wear thin over hundreds of thousands of kilometres and are turned on a lathe to restore their shape, until they're too thin and are replaced.
details.howItWorks: The rear driving wheel on the left is linked by the coupling rod to the others, adding its grip to theirs. It sits just ahead of the firebox. Like the others, its tyre has a flange on the inside to keep it on the rails.
keyNumbers: About 2.03 m diameter
Coupled wheelbase about 4.4 m
Tyre roughly 14 cm wide
details.madeOf: Cast steel spoked centre with a steel tyre and balance weight.

parts.name: Driving wheel (rear, left)

parts.description: Carrying wheel under the cab that supports the weight of the big, wide firebox.

details.didYouKnow: Adding trailing wheels to make room for a wide firebox is what turned the older 4-6-0 express engines into the much more powerful Pacifics.
details.howItWorks: The trailing wheels under the cab carry the weight of the large firebox, which is too wide to fit between the big driving wheels. This is the "2" in 4-6-2. The axle can slide a little sideways so the long engine can still take curves.
keyNumbers: About 1.12 m diameter
Carries roughly 15 to 20 tonnes
Lets the firebox be wide and deep
details.madeOf: Cast steel wheel centre with a shrunk-on steel tyre, in a sliding axlebox.

parts.name: Trailing wheel (left)

parts.description: Small guiding wheel on the front bogie, which swivels to lead the engine smoothly into curves.

details.didYouKnow: Because the two wheels on an axle are fixed together, coned treads are what let a railway wheelset go round a curve: the outer wheel rides on its bigger part.
details.howItWorks: The front right bogie wheel is pressed onto the same axle as the front left, so both wheels turn together. The treads are slightly coned, which steers the wheelset back to the centre of the track. The flange on the inside only touches the rail on tight curves.
keyNumbers: About 0.97 m diameter
Flange about 3 cm deep
Coned tread of about 1 in 20
details.madeOf: Cast steel centre and steel tyre, pressed onto a solid steel axle.

parts.name: Bogie wheel (front, right)

parts.description: Small guiding wheel on the front bogie, which swivels to lead the engine smoothly into curves.

details.didYouKnow: Engine crews walked round with an oil can and a hammer: tapping a wheel tyre and listening for a clear ring was a quick way to spot a cracked one.
details.howItWorks: The rear right bogie wheel completes the four-wheeled bogie. Together the four carry the weight of the smokebox and cylinders and guide the engine. Their axleboxes are oiled and checked by the crew before every trip.
keyNumbers: About 0.97 m diameter
One of four bogie wheels
Axle load roughly 10 tonnes
details.madeOf: Cast steel centre and steel tyre on a solid steel axle, running in oil-lubricated bronze axleboxes.

parts.name: Bogie wheel (rear, right)

parts.description: One of six 2-metre driving wheels; the pistons turn them through the rods and they push the train along.

details.didYouKnow: A slipping engine could spin its driving wheels furiously while hardly moving, which is why drivers opened the regulator gently and used sand on wet or leafy rails.
details.howItWorks: The front right driving wheel shares an axle with the front left one, and its crank pin is set a quarter turn round from the left side's. It's coupled to the other right-hand wheels by the right coupling rod. Sand can be blown under it from the sandbox to stop it slipping on wet rails.
keyNumbers: About 2.03 m diameter
Crank 90° from the left side
About 7 turns a second at 100 mph
details.madeOf: Cast steel centre, shrunk-on steel tyre and a balance weight.

parts.name: Driving wheel (leading, right)

parts.description: One of six 2-metre driving wheels; the pistons turn them through the rods and they push the train along.

details.didYouKnow: At Mallard's record 126 mph, its 6 ft 8 in driving wheels were turning more than 500 times a minute.
details.howItWorks: The middle right wheel takes the drive from the right connecting rod, a quarter turn out of step with the left side. Between them, the two sides keep the axle turning smoothly. This axle carries the most load of any on the engine.
keyNumbers: About 2.03 m diameter
Driven directly by the right cylinder
Axle load around 22 tonnes
details.madeOf: Cast steel spoked centre, steel tyre, large balance weight and a pressed-in crank pin.

parts.name: Driving wheel (middle, right)

parts.description: One of six 2-metre driving wheels; the pistons turn them through the rods and they push the train along.

details.didYouKnow: The "6" in 4-6-2 is these six wheels, three on each side; the Whyte system counts wheels, not axles.
details.howItWorks: The rear right driving wheel completes the set of six. With all six coupled, the engine can put about two-thirds of its weight onto driving wheels for grip. It runs in an axlebox that can slide up and down in the frames on springs.
keyNumbers: About 2.03 m diameter
One of six coupled driving wheels
Around 65 tonnes on the six together
details.madeOf: Cast steel centre and steel tyre with a balance weight.

parts.name: Driving wheel (rear, right)

parts.description: Carrying wheel under the cab that supports the weight of the big, wide firebox.

details.didYouKnow: On the A3 the trailing axle ran in a sliding frame called a Cartazzi axlebox, named after the Italian engineer who designed it.
details.howItWorks: The right trailing wheel pairs with the left on a single axle under the back of the engine. Together they support the firebox and cab. They don't drive; they simply carry weight and guide.
keyNumbers: About 1.12 m diameter
Unpowered carrying wheel
Sits beneath the cab floor
details.madeOf: Cast steel centre and steel tyre on a solid steel axle.

parts.name: Trailing wheel (right)

parts.description: Long steel plate frame that everything bolts to; the axles ride in slots in it on springs.

details.didYouKnow: Frames flex and crack over years of pounding, so engines that run for decades sometimes end up with new frames, which raises the question of whether it's still the same locomotive.
details.howItWorks: The left frame is a long steel plate running the length of the engine, standing on edge. The axles ride in slots cut into it, on springs, and the cylinders, boiler and cab are all bolted to it. With the right frame and cross-stretchers between them, it forms the engine's backbone.
keyNumbers: About 12.5 m long
Plate about 2.5 to 3 cm thick
Carries over 90 tonnes of engine
details.madeOf: Rolled steel plate, cut and machined, joined to the other frame by steel cross-stretchers.

parts.name: Main frame (left)

parts.description: Long steel plate frame that everything bolts to; the axles ride in slots in it on springs.

details.didYouKnow: Before a new engine is built, the frames are laid out and drilled first, and everything else is assembled on top of them.
details.howItWorks: The right frame mirrors the left and holds the other ends of the axles. The two frames are held exactly parallel and square, so the axles stay perfectly lined up. The middle cylinder on three-cylinder engines like the A3 sits between them.
keyNumbers: About 12.5 m long
Roughly 1.2 m apart
Inside the wheels on most British engines
details.madeOf: Rolled steel plate, bolted to stretchers, with hornguides for the axleboxes.

parts.name: Main frame (right)

parts.description: Walkway along each side above the wheels, and the floor of the cab at the back.

details.didYouKnow: Drivers and firemen are called "footplatemen" in Britain after the floor they stand on.
details.howItWorks: The running plate is the ledge running along both sides above the wheels. Crews walk along it to reach the smokebox and lamps, and it covers the tops of the wheels. At the back it becomes the footplate, the floor of the cab where the crew stand.
keyNumbers: About 2.1 m above the rails
The full 2.75 m width of the engine
Steps lead up at the front and cab
details.madeOf: Steel plate on brackets from the frames, often with a raised edge painted in a lining colour.

parts.name: Running plate

parts.description: Frame of the four-wheeled leading truck, pivoted under the cylinders and free to slide sideways on curves.

details.didYouKnow: A well-designed bogie made the difference between an engine that rode smoothly at 100 mph and one that swayed alarmingly.
details.howItWorks: The bogie frame holds the four leading wheels and turns on a pin under the cylinders. Springs centre it on straight track and let it move sideways on curves. It also carries part of the front of the engine's weight.
keyNumbers: About 2 m between its axles
Side movement of a few centimetres
Carries roughly 20 tonnes
details.madeOf: Steel plates and castings with laminated leaf springs or coil springs and a centre pivot.

parts.name: Front bogie frame

parts.description: Stout cross-beam at the front, painted red, carrying the buffers and coupling.

details.didYouKnow: Buffer beams on British engines were almost always painted bright red, so the front end stood out to shunters and track workers in a gloomy yard.
details.howItWorks: The buffer beam is the strong cross-beam at the very front of the frames. It carries the buffers, the coupling and the lamp irons, and it takes the shove when the engine buffers up to a train. It's painted red so it stands out.
keyNumbers: 2.75 m wide
Buffer height about 1.05 m above the rails
Takes pushes of many tonnes
details.madeOf: Thick steel plate or a steel channel, riveted or bolted to the ends of the frames.

parts.name: Buffer beam

parts.description: Spring-loaded buffer that cushions the knocks between the engine and whatever it meets.

details.didYouKnow: On curves the buffers of two vehicles slide across each other's faces, which is why the heads are large and kept greased.
details.howItWorks: Each buffer is a plunger with a round head, pushed out by a strong spring inside its casing. When the engine meets a carriage, the buffers squash and cushion the shock. They also keep the gap between vehicles steady when the train is pushed or braking.
keyNumbers: About 1.74 m apart, centre to centre
Head about 45 cm across
Can compress by around 10 cm
details.madeOf: Cast or forged steel casing, steel plunger and head, with a heavy spring inside.

parts.name: Buffer (left)

parts.description: Spring-loaded buffer that cushions the knocks between the engine and whatever it meets.

details.didYouKnow: Buffers and screw couplings are why British trains were coupled by hand, with a shunter climbing between the buffers to lift the link onto the hook.
details.howItWorks: The right buffer pairs with the left, so a carriage's buffers meet two heads at the same height. With the coupling screwed tight, the buffers just touch, which stops the train snatching and banging as it speeds up and slows down. Their faces are greased to slide freely.
keyNumbers: About 1.05 m above the rails
One of a pair
Standard height across British railways
details.madeOf: Steel casing, plunger and head with a coil spring or rubber blocks inside.

parts.name: Buffer (right)

parts.description: Hook and screw coupling for attaching to a train or another engine at the front.

details.didYouKnow: Two engines coupled together to pull one heavy train is called double-heading, and the front coupling makes it possible.
details.howItWorks: The coupling is a strong hook on the buffer beam with a screw-adjusted link hanging from it. The shunter drops the link over the hook of the next vehicle and turns the screw handle to pull the two together until the buffers touch. An engine usually pulls from the back, but this front coupling lets it be attached to another engine or a train when needed.
keyNumbers: Rated for pulls of tens of tonnes
Screw shortens the link by several centimetres
Hung from the centre of the buffer beam
details.madeOf: Forged steel hook and links with a threaded steel screw and handle.

parts.name: Front coupling

parts.description: Steel bar pinned to both the engine and the tender, carrying the whole pull of the train.

details.didYouKnow: The engine and tender are never meant to be separated in service, so the drawbar is pinned rather than hooked, and taking it off is a job for the shed.
details.howItWorks: The drawbar is a heavy steel bar pinned at one end to the engine and at the other to the tender. All the pulling force of the engine passes through it on its way to the train behind. Side buffers between the engine and tender keep the pair steady and stop them snaking.
keyNumbers: Carries pulls of roughly 15 tonnes or more
Less than a metre long
Usually backed up by safety links
details.madeOf: Forged high-strength steel, with steel pins through each end.

parts.name: Drawbar

parts.description: Underframe of the tender, carrying the tank on its wheels and springs.

details.didYouKnow: Some LNER tenders had a narrow corridor down one side so a fresh crew could walk through from the train and take over at speed on non-stop runs.
details.howItWorks: The tender frame is the underframe that carries the water tank, the coal and the brakes. Its axles ride in axleboxes on springs, like the engine's. At the front it holds the drawbar, and at the back the buffers and coupling to the train.
keyNumbers: About 8 m long
Carries over 50 tonnes when full
Rides on wheels about 1.26 m across
details.madeOf: Steel plate frames and cross-members, riveted together.

parts.name: Tender frame

parts.description: Welded tank holding about 23,000 litres of water, wrapped round the base and back of the coal space.

details.didYouKnow: A water scoop at about 60 mph could pick up a few thousand litres from a quarter-mile trough in seconds.
details.howItWorks: The tank carries the water the boiler turns into steam, wrapped around the bottom and back of the coal space. Injectors on the engine use a jet of steam to force water from the tank into the boiler against its own pressure. Some tanks had a scoop underneath that could be lowered to pick up water from long troughs between the rails without stopping.
keyNumbers: About 23,000 litres (5,000 gallons)
Water weighs about 23 tonnes when full
A Pacific can use roughly 100 litres a kilometre
details.madeOf: Riveted or welded steel plate, with internal baffles to stop the water sloshing.

parts.name: Water tank

parts.description: Raised side sheet that forms one wall of the coal space on top of the tank.

details.didYouKnow: Tender sides often carried the railway's name in large letters, like "LNER", so they doubled as a moving advertisement.
details.howItWorks: The left side sheet rises above the tank to form one wall of the coal space. It lets the tender hold a big heap of coal without it spilling off on curves. It's shaped to match the cab sides so the engine and tender look like one.
keyNumbers: About 5 m long
Roughly 1 m tall above the tank
Top level with the cab sides
details.madeOf: Steel plate, painted in the engine's livery and lined.

parts.name: Coal bunker side (left)

parts.description: Raised side sheet that forms one wall of the coal space on top of the tank.

details.didYouKnow: Coal could be loaded so high it was heaped above the sides, and a jolt at the coaling stage sometimes sent lumps bouncing onto the track.
details.howItWorks: The right side sheet mirrors the left, closing the other side of the coal space. Between them the sides, the coal plate at the front and the raised tank at the back form a big open bunker. Its edge is often turned in slightly to keep coal from falling off.
keyNumbers: About 5 m long
One of a matched pair
Helps hold about 9 tonnes of coal
details.madeOf: Steel plate, painted and lined to match the engine.

parts.name: Coal bunker side (right)

parts.description: Front wall of the coal space facing the cab, with small doors at the bottom where the fireman shovels from.

details.didYouKnow: A good fireman could shovel coal from here to exactly the right spot on the grate in a single swing, without even looking.
details.howItWorks: The front wall of the coal space faces the cab, with small doors at the bottom called the coal hole. The fireman shovels from there, and as the pile goes down coal slides forward on the sloping floor. On long runs the fireman sometimes climbed up to pull coal forward from the back.
keyNumbers: About 2.7 m wide
Coal doors near floor level
Just a short step from the firehole

details.didYouKnow: Only around 6 to 8 percent of the coal's energy ended up pulling the train; the rest went up the chimney or out as heat.
details.howItWorks: The coal is the engine's fuel, burned in the firebox to boil the water. A load lasts a few hundred kilometres of hard running, and water runs out long before coal does. Coal quality matters a lot: hard, clean coal made steam easily, while poor coal clogged the fire.
keyNumbers: About 9 tonnes on an LNER corridor tender
Roughly 10 to 15 kg burned for every kilometre
Energy roughly 30 megajoules per kilogram

One of six tender wheels here
Axle load roughly 18 tonnes when full

Middle of three axles

summary: A 4-6-2 "Pacific" express steam locomotive and its tender, like the LNER A3: a coal fire boils water in a long boiler, and the steam drives two pistons that turn six 2-metre driving wheels, pulling a heavy train at up to about 160 km/h.
